items.definition: One move made to push a decision, such as a deadline, a discount or a display of authority.
items.example: The second call was a pressure tactic: it moved the deadline by one hour.

items.definition: Everyone agreeing freely to something, every time. A clear no is a complete answer that needs no follow-up.
items.example: Consent has to be clear on both sides, and a no is always a complete answer.

items.definition: A line you draw around your time, energy, body or values, and say out loud so other people can respect it.
items.example: Her boundary was simple: no phone calls after ten.

items.definition: A pattern in which one person keeps control over another by limiting their money, their time or their contact with other people.
items.example: The pattern of coercive control is recognised by what it restricts, not by what it says.

items.definition: The use of pressure, ambiguity or emotion to move a person into a decision that does not serve them, without giving a real choice.
items.example: It was manipulation: he offered her two options and made the wrong one impossible.

items.definition: An error in the shape of an argument, a move that breaks the reasoning instead of answering the claim.
items.example: Calling the move a fallacy describes it; it does not insult the person.

items.definition: The presenting of two options as if no other option existed.
items.example: Either we cut the budget by a third, or the service stops — that is a false dilemma.

items.definition: A question that carries its own answer inside its wording.
items.example: When will you stop making excuses? is a loaded question.

items.definition: The moving of the criterion after the other side has met it.
items.example: Three sources were required, then written external sources were required: that was goalpost shifting.

items.definition: The replacing of a reason with a feeling, and the treatment of the feeling as the answer.
items.example: After everything I have done for this team was an appeal to emotion, not a reason.

items.definition: The replacing of a reason with the title or the status of the person who offers it.
items.example: The chief engineer says it is safe was an appeal to authority, because no evidence was shown.

items.definition: An argument that nobody made, set up so that it can be knocked down easily.
items.example: So you want to drop the whole project was a straw man; the speaker had only said the schedule was short.

items.definition: An attack on the person instead of on the claim.
items.example: You did not read the report, so your opinion does not count is an ad hominem.

items.definition: The turning of an answer into an answer about somebody else.
items.example: You did the same thing last year is whataboutism: it answers nothing.

items.definition: The formal name for whataboutism; it means "you too".
items.example: The reply was a tu quoque: it pointed at the other person's record and stayed there.

items.definition: Money, time or effort that has already been spent, and which is used as a reason to continue.
items.example: The sunk cost of the training was the argument for staying in the job.

items.definition: The choice of words around a fact, which changes how the fact feels.
items.example: The framing changed nothing: 400 a month is the same money as 4,800 a year.

items.definition: A reply that takes the point that was made and answers it with a reason.
items.example: The rebuttal gave the reason and asked for the same test on the other side.

items.definition: Agreement produced not by open discussion but by arranging the information environment so one conclusion appears natural.
The power to decide which topics the public thinks about, exercised through selection and emphasis in coverage.
Influence over how a topic is understood: which frames, words and experts define it.
Influence achieved through attraction and information rather than force or payment.
Withholding one's own views to avoid social, professional or legal consequences.
The tendency of a cohesive group to converge on one view and suppress doubt in order to preserve harmony.
A statement that fixes the exact meaning of a word, so that everybody uses it the same way.
items.example: The definition of a tolerance is written at the top of the drawing, and every measurement follows it.

items.definition: A statement that a system takes as true and never proves for itself.
items.example: The axioms are the starting points of the proof, and everything after them is derived.

items.definition: The step that carries you from what is already accepted to what follows from it.
items.example: By logical deduction, the conclusion follows from the premises, and nothing else is needed.

items.definition: A working idea of how something behaves, kept by the writer and never written as a rule.
items.example: The writer has a model of how a nervous engineer behaves, and every scene is built on it.

items.definition: The written record of a reasoning, in which every line follows from the lines above it.
items.example: The proof is short, and any reader can check it line by line.

items.definition: A statement that an argument starts from and takes as given.
items.example: The premise is wrong, so the conclusion is right only in the proof.

items.definition: The property of a set of axioms that do not contradict one another.
items.example: The two rules cannot both be true, so the set of rules is not consistent.

items.definition: The quality of a situation that could happen, even when it did not.
items.example: The story has plausibility, and the details of the rule are still missing.

items.definition: The point of view a story is told from, which decides what the reader can and cannot see.
items.example: From the perspective of the night engineer, the quiet building is the whole story.

items.definition: A place in a text where two meanings are held at once and the reader must choose one.
items.example: The ambiguity in the last line is deliberate, and the reader has to settle it.

items.definition: The meaning a reader gives a result in their own work once they have understood it.
items.example: The interpretation is the last step: the number is correct, and now it has to mean something on the night shift.

items.definition: Using external tools to store, compute or retrieve information so that your own mind does not have to.
The shared system by which a group, or a person and a tool, divides the work of remembering who knows what.
The disciplined practice of examining claims, evidence and reasoning before accepting a conclusion.
The ability to form, hold and explain your own views without needing them to be pre-approved by an authority or a tool.
The gradual loss of a skill when it is no longer practiced because a machine performs it instead.
